title: Most Zugzwang ever Zugzwanged
summary: Place both bishops correctly before using the king to restrict the rook to a fork or a pin.

nodes.question: Where should the attacked bishop go?
nodes.explanation: White has Kc1, Ba2, Ba3 and f3 against Ka1 and Rb7. Be6 preserves a bishop net that Bg8 would not create.

branches.title: Build the bishop net, then fork the rook
commentary: Begin from the complete six-piece source board. The central line includes the intervening Kd2 and ...Rxf3 before Ke2.
Be6 moves the attacked a2 bishop to the diagonal needed for the net.
Rb3 attacks Ba3 and f3, setting up the rook’s defensive resource.
Bd6 moves the a3 bishop while preserving coordination with Be6.
Rc3+ checks along the c-file, forcing the king to respond.
Kd2 answers the check and approaches the rook.
Rxf3 collects the pawn, but places the rook where the white king can restrict it.
Ke2 attacks Rf3 and helps confine the rook. The two bishops control most of its other safe destinations.
Rf6 is the source’s selected flight square on the a1–f6 diagonal.
Be5+ checks Ka1 while attacking Rf6. White has an exact win at the fork; no unshown king reply is assumed.
branches.explanation: Be5+ checks Ka1 while attacking Rf6. White has an exact win at the fork; no unshown king reply is assumed.

branches.title: The rook chooses the pin square
commentary: Follow the same source setup and compare the rook’s other illustrated destination.
Be6 places the first bishop precisely.
Rb3 attacks the pawn and the other bishop.
Bd6 forms the bishop net.
Rc3+ checks the king.
Kd2 answers that check.
Rxf3 takes the pawn.
Ke2 attacks the rook and controls nearby squares.
Rc3 retreats onto the same diagonal as Ka1.
Be5 pins Rc3 to Ka1. The rook now blocks the bishop’s checking line.
Kb2 is the illustrated king approach, defending the rook.
Kd2 adds a second attack on Rc3. The checked position is winning; the lesson stops before inventing a final rook reply.
branches.explanation: Kd2 adds a second attack on Rc3. The checked position is winning; the lesson stops before inventing a final rook reply.

branches.title: Retreat to g8 and accept the rook
commentary: Compare the source’s natural long bishop retreat and the tempting rook capture.
Bg8 gives up White’s forced win by allowing the rook’s stalemate defense.
Rb3 offers the rook while attacking the bishop and pawn.
Bxb3 is actual stalemate. Kc1 covers b1/b2, Bb3 covers a2, and Ka1 is not in check.
branches.explanation: Bxb3 is actual stalemate. Kc1 covers b1/b2, Bb3 covers a2, and Ka1 is not in check.

exercises.prompt: Why is the bishop’s retreat square important?
exercises.answer: Be6 and Bd6 control enough rook destinations for Ke2 to force a diagonal fork or pin. Bg8 permits the checking rook defense and a stalemate capture instead.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between Be5+ and Be5?
exercises.answer: Against Rf6, Be5+ checks the king and forks the rook. Against Rc3, the rook blocks the bishop’s line to Ka1 and is pinned, so Be5 is not check.

startContext: The complete six-piece source root and selected bishop-net branches are visually reconstructed. The saved sequence includes Kd2 after ...Rc3+, then ...Rxf3 Ke2; those intervening moves are preserved rather than treating Ke2 as a jump from c1. The skewer/fork endpoints are exact wins, not immediate mates. The advertising overlay is outside the chess lesson.
verification_scope: Saved board images reviewed manually. Every encoded intermediate position and endpoint is checked against the tablebase. Selected instructive variations, not an exhaustive tree of all legal defenses.
